title: Variable scope and storage
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates can reason about which code can see a variable and how long it lives—global vs local vs static—because mistakes here cause wrong outputs and shared-state bugs.

phases.goal: Establish that declaration site controls both visibility (scope) and lifetime (storage duration), and define global vs local.

must_hit.point: A global variable is declared outside every function and is visible to all of them.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says globals sit outside functions and any function can reach them.

must_hit.point: A local variable is declared inside a function or block and is visible only there.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says locals are confined to their function or block.

must_hit.point: Where a variable is declared controls which code can see it (scope) and how long it lives (lifetime / storage duration).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates the two concerns: who can name it vs how long the object exists.

probes: What is the difference between a global variable and a local variable in C++?

hints.1: Think about where each is declared relative to functions.
hints.2: One is outside every function; the other is inside a function or block.
hints.3: Global: outside all functions, visible to all; local: inside a function/block, visible only there.

phases.goal: Show how nested scopes resolve names via shadowing, and how static locals retain value across calls while staying function-private.

must_hit.point: An inner declaration may reuse a name from an outer scope; the inner name shadows the outer one within its block, and an unqualified use refers to the nearest enclosing declaration.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes shadowing and nearest-enclosing resolution, e.g. nested x printing the innermost first.

must_hit.point: A static local variable lives inside a function but, unlike an ordinary local, retains its value between calls; it is initialised once and persists for the whole run of the program while staying visible only inside its function.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says init once, survives across calls, still only visible in that function.

must_hit.point: Each call recreates an ordinary local afresh, while a static local carries over across calls.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts ordinary local always reset vs static counting up across successive calls.

probes: If the same name is declared in nested blocks, which declaration does an unqualified use refer to?
What happens to a static local's value across multiple calls to the same function?

hints.1: Compare ordinary locals to static locals on the second and third call.
hints.2: For names: walk outward from the use site; for static: ask whether it is re-created each call.
hints.3: Nearest enclosing declaration wins for shadowing; static is initialised once and retains its value between calls while remaining visible only inside its function.

phases.goal: State when globals are convenient versus why locals are preferred, and what a static local uniquely combines.

must_hit.point: Globals are convenient when a value must be reachable by many functions, but they can be changed from anywhere, which is why locals are preferred whenever a value is needed in only one place.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions multi-function reachability vs uncontrolled mutation; prefers locals for single-place use.

must_hit.point: A static local combines a local's narrow visibility with a global's lifetime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly pairs narrow visibility with program-long lifetime.

probes: When would you use a global versus a local, and what risk do globals introduce?
What does a static local give you that neither a plain local nor a global alone provides?

hints.1: Ask who needs to see the value and who might accidentally change it.
hints.2: Globals: shared reach; locals: confined; static local: confined name, long life.
hints.3: Prefer locals for one-place use; globals when many functions need the value but anything can mutate them; static local = local visibility + global lifetime.

phases.goal: Apply scope/lifetime rules to predict which binding is used and how values evolve across calls.

must_hit.point: In nested scopes that each declare x, printing at each level yields the innermost binding first, then the enclosing function's binding, with the global remaining outside those blocks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the nested-x example: innermost block, then main's x, then global outside.

must_hit.point: Across repeated calls, an ordinary local is recreated each time while a static local increments and retains its prior value between calls.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes ordinary local reset each call vs static carrying over across successive calls.

probes: Given nested declarations of the same name at global, function, and block scope, what does each unqualified print refer to?
If a function has both an ordinary local and a static local that is incremented each call, what differs between the first and third call?

hints.1: Resolve each print from the use site outward.
hints.2: Track which variables are recreated vs which persist across calls.
hints.3: Innermost shadowing wins at each level; ordinary locals reset every call while the static local keeps counting across calls.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use a global when many functions must reach the same value; prefer a local whenever the value is needed in only one place, because a global can be changed from anywhere.
An ordinary local is recreated each call; a static local keeps local-only visibility but retains its value for the whole program run—local visibility with global lifetime.

gotchas.trap: Assuming an unqualified name always means the global (or the function-level) variable when an inner block redeclares the same name.
gotchas.correction: The inner name shadows the outer one within its block; an unqualified use refers to the nearest enclosing declaration.

gotchas.trap: Treating a static local like an ordinary local that resets on every call, or like a global that every function can see.
gotchas.correction: A static local is initialised once, retains its value between calls for the whole program run, and stays visible only inside its function.
